source.version: arXiv:2607.11837v1 [cs.HC], 13 Jul 2026, as stamped on PDF p. 1. The July 2024 ACM template footer is not treated as a publication date.

studies.label: FIERO versus Google Docs collaborative superhero-story writing

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 13, Section 4.1 (randomized participants); PDF p. 41, Appendix A, Table 1 heading and note (questionnaire participants only)
counts_source.quote: In this between-subjects experiment, 60 participants were randomly assigned to either a story creation group or a card game-based story creation group. ... (n=30 per group) ... (N=60).

arms.name: FIERO
arms.description: Face-to-face collaborative writing using physical narrative cards and the FIERO interface, with AI-generated images, optional decision suggestions, story suggestions and polishing. AI remained available during production of the final story. The analyzed people count here is the questionnaire count, not the scored-story sample (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; PDF p. 41, Table 1; PDF p. 48, Appendix E.2).

arms.name: Control (Google Docs)
arms.description: Face-to-face collaborative writing in a shared Google Docs page, with individual drafts, mutual review, discussion and final story integration; no AI or physical cards. The narrative tasks and round timing matched FIERO. The analyzed people count here is the questionnaire count, not the scored-story sample (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; PDF p. 34, Section 6.6.1; PDF p. 41, Table 1; PDF pp. 47-48, Appendix E.1).

studies.task: Teams of three collaboratively create a superhero story through hero creation, villain and scene development, weapon and climax development, and final narrative integration (PDF p. 13, Section 4.1).

ai_tool.name: FIERO: GPT-4 for text assistance; GPT-4o image model (gpt-4o-image) for images
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 12, Section 3.4; PDF p. 49, Appendix F.1, Table 5. Model release years are not printed.

preregistration.where: Not stated in the article or Appendices A-H.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Claude Opus 4.5 as judge. Originality, innovative concepts, uniqueness, fresh perspectives and imaginative content (PDF pp. 15-16, Section 4.2.2; PDF p. 46, Appendix D). Each FIERO story is compared with each control story in both AB and BA orders; inconsistent judgments become draws. The models judge the same team-produced stories, so evaluator variants are dependent measurements of one sample (PDF p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Reported statistic: net advantage of FIERO over Control, in percentage points of pairwise preference; the paper prints these with a percent sign. It is a preference-rate margin, not a continuous rating or a standardized effect.

stats.difference_is: FIERO minus Control net advantage in pairwise preference, in the printed percent units; no rescaling or calculation.

sources.locator: PDF p. 27, Section 5.4.1; pairing protocol in PDF p. 17, Section 4.5.2
sources.quote: the FIERO condition achieved win rates of 60.5% (49/81) with Claude, 56.8% (46/81) with Gemini, and 76.5% (62/81) with GPT-5.2.

sources.locator: PDF p. 29, Figure 14 caption
sources.quote: Creativity exhibited the greatest inter-judge variability, with Gemini favoring FIERO (+50.6%) while Claude and GPT-5.2 favored the control condition (-27.2% and -7.4%).

estimates.notes: The signed net advantage is printed in the Figure 14 caption, so it is available without reading a plotted cell. The caption associates the two negative values with Claude and GPT-5.2 in the stated order. The participant counts for the scored-story analysis are not printed and are left null; the questionnaire counts are not substituted. The pair count is the printed comparison denominator in Section 5.4.1, with the cross-arm pairing protocol specified in Section 4.5.2. The same stories recur across pairs. No dimension-specific inferential test, standard error or confidence interval is reported.

Character depth, human-like emotions and motivations, relatability, emotional expression and psychological realism (PDF p. 15, Section 4.2.2; PDF pp. 45-46, Appendix D). Each FIERO story is compared with each control story in both AB and BA orders; inconsistent judgments become draws. The models judge the same team-produced stories, so evaluator variants are dependent measurements of one sample (PDF p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Reported statistic: net advantage of FIERO over Control, in percentage points of pairwise preference; the paper prints these with a percent sign. It is a preference-rate margin, not a continuous rating or a standardized effect.

stats.difference_is: FIERO minus Control net advantage in pairwise preference, in the printed percent units; no rescaling or calculation.

estimates.notes: The participant counts for the scored-story analysis are not printed and are left null; the questionnaire counts are not substituted. No win-rate difference, standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval, degrees of freedom or standardized effect is calculated. The test is retained as printed without reconstructing its contingency table or null hypothesis. Section 5.4.1/Figure 13 and the Overall row of Figure 14 may summarize distinct judging outputs or contain a reporting error; Appendix D (PDF p. 47) lists both Overall and Final_Winner without mapping them to these summaries. This record shares the stories and form outcome with the corresponding Overall Preference dimension record and is not independent evidence.

open_items: The paper reports ten teams of three per arm (PDF p. 16, Section 4.4), but evaluates nine texts per arm (PDF p. 17, Section 4.5.2). It does not identify omitted teams/texts or print the participant headcount represented in these texts. Estimate-level people counts remain null.

Random allocation of participants is stated on PDF p. 13, Section 4.1, but the allocation procedure and timing of team formation relative to randomization are unspecified. Individual is retained as the stated assignment unit; team or session randomization is not inferred.

No participant- or team-adjusted uncertainty is provided for the scored stories. The overall chi-squared tests reuse stories across pairs, and no degrees of freedom or contingency-table specification is supplied (PDF pp. 17, 27). Story identifiers and judgments would be needed to resolve dependence.

Judge-specific point estimates for most dimensions, control win rates and draw proportions are available only in Figures 13-14. Prose ranges without explicit judge attribution are not converted into individual estimates; the corresponding numeric fields remain null.

The relationship between the overall comparison on PDF p. 27, Section 5.4.1/Figure 13, and the Overall Preference dimension on PDF p. 29, Section 5.4.2/Figure 14, is unexplained. Appendix D on PDF p. 47 includes both Overall and Final_Winner fields. These summaries must not be combined or assigned each other's tests without clarification.

No continuous participant-, team- or output-level creativity-score standard deviations are supplied, and no standardized story-quality effect is printed. Preference percentages alone are not standardized effects.
Model release years, study country and preregistration are not stated. The AI tool year is null and country/preregistration are coded not_stated rather than inferred.

The screening form flags unexplained questionnaire item denominators or response processing. The declared questionnaire counts are retained as study-level counts only and are not used for the scored-story analysis (PDF p. 14, Section 4.2.1; PDF p. 41, Table 2).
Appendix H on PDF p. 51 names system, card and prompt artifacts, but does not explicitly identify participant-level data or the story-pair judgments needed to address these gaps.
notes: Extractor A read the complete markdown from start to end, including references and all appendices, and checked every cited PDF page with PyMuPDF. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. All quotes are copied from PDF text with whitespace normalized. Study-level n_analyzed and arm n_analyzed refer to questionnaires only (PDF p. 41, Table 1); the scored-story sample has no printed people count. Arm-specific randomized counts are not separately printed and remain null. The paper states randomization of individuals; clusters_per_arm is empty because randomized clusters are not established. Population is mixed: students and non-students without professional creative-writing backgrounds (PDF p. 16, Section 4.4); country is not inferred from affiliations. AI role is other because FIERO combines image generation, decision support and refinement (PDF pp. 12, 48-50). The effect is of the full FIERO package, including physical cards, the game interface and AI, versus collaborative writing in Google Docs; the paper explicitly acknowledges this bundled comparison (PDF p. 34, Section 6.6.1). Google Docs is the study's ordinary collaborative-writing baseline; human collaboration is present in both arms, supporting ai_vs_bau. LLM evaluator variants score the same outputs and are not separate studies or independent samples. Each scored story dimension is retained for each evaluator, including records whose figure-only point estimates are null. The separately labeled overall comparison and Overall Preference dimension are both retained without assuming equivalence. Numbers printed in prose and the Figure 14 caption are eligible for transcription; numbers requiring reading a plotted cell or bar label are not copied. Net advantages are retained in their printed percent units and are not divided by one hundred. No effect size, standard error, headcount or unprinted difference was calculated. No quantitative across-people diversity measure or later unassisted task is reported. No shared sample is identified in the screening form or paper; shared_sample is null, not an assertion that overlap is impossible. The appendix describes no additional eligible study.
